---
title: "Ordinal regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

An ordinal response has ordered categories but no defensible numerical spacing. We use **MegaVeridicality v1**, the *no*–*maybe*–*yes* veridicality judgments described by White and Rawlins ([2018 paper](https://ling.auf.net/lingbuzz/004012/current.pdf); [CC BY-SA project release](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-veridicality/)). Each row is one judgment for a verb, polarity, task, item, and task-specific respondent. The direct and conditional tasks recruited separate samples; the task prefix on `respondent_id` prevents 29 reused numeric labels from becoming false repeated measurements.

```{r}
#| label: load-megaveridicality
#| echo: true
library(ordinal)
mv <- read.csv("data/megaveridicality/megaveridicality-v1-active-native.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(mv) == 14951L, length(unique(mv$verb)) == 375L,
          length(unique(mv$respondent_id)) == 319L)
mv$outcome <- ordered(mv$response, levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes"))
mv$polarity <- factor(mv$polarity, levels = c("positive", "negative"))
mv$task <- factor(mv$task, levels = c("direct", "conditional"))
fit <- clm(outcome ~ polarity * task, data = mv, link = "logit", Hess = TRUE)
coef(summary(fit))
```

## Cumulative logits

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_1<\kappa_2$ and linear predictor $\eta_i$,

$$
\operatorname{logit}\mathbb{P}(Y_i\leq c)=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

With the logistic CDF $F$, the category probabilities are

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{maybe})=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

The model preserves order without assigning equal distances to the labels.

## Interpreting one coefficient at both boundaries

A positive coefficient increases the linear predictor and shifts probability toward higher responses. Under proportional odds, the same coefficient applies to *maybe* or *yes* versus *no* and to *yes* versus *no* or *maybe*. It does not imply an equal change in each category probability, which is why the complete fitted distribution remains the primary interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: ordinal-raw-and-fitted
#| echo: true
grid <- expand.grid(polarity = levels(mv$polarity), task = levels(mv$task))
fitted_matrix <- predict(fit, newdata = grid, type = "prob")$fit
fitted_long <- data.frame(
  grid[rep(seq_len(nrow(grid)), each = ncol(fitted_matrix)), ],
  response = factor(rep(colnames(fitted_matrix), times = nrow(grid)),
                    levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")),
  fitted_probability = as.vector(t(fitted_matrix))
)
raw <- as.data.frame(table(mv$polarity, mv$task, mv$outcome,
                           dnn = c("polarity", "task", "response")))
names(raw)[[4L]] <- "responses"
raw$empirical_probability <- ave(raw$responses, raw$polarity, raw$task,
                                 FUN = function(x) x / sum(x))
display <- merge(raw, fitted_long, by = c("polarity", "task", "response"))
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-ordinal-fit
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(display, aes(response, group = polarity)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = empirical_probability, shape = polarity), size = 2,
             position = position_dodge(width = .18)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_probability, linetype = polarity),
            color = "#1F5A85", linewidth = .75,
            position = position_dodge(width = .18)) +
  facet_wrap(~ task) +
  labs(x = "Response", y = "Response probability", shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Checking the shared-shift restriction

The proportional-odds model requires the same predictor shift at both boundaries. Two binary regressions expose how strained that restriction is here.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-check
#| echo: true
above_no <- glm(I(as.integer(outcome) > 1L) ~ polarity * task,
                binomial(), mv)
yes <- glm(I(as.integer(outcome) > 2L) ~ polarity * task,
           binomial(), mv)
rbind(`maybe-or-yes versus no` = coef(above_no),
      `yes versus no-or-maybe` = coef(yes))
```

The negative-polarity and polarity-by-task coefficients differ across boundaries, so one shared location shift is a useful baseline but an imperfect description. The fit is a population teaching model, not the paper's responsivity analysis and not a latent verb classification. It also omits respondent and verb dependence, which the later ordinal mixed-model page addresses.
